title: How a nonprofit should write an about page
metaTitle: How to write a nonprofit about page
excerpt: Name who runs the program and why that should matter to a donor or a participant. Keep a founding story only when it changes the decision to give or join.
alt: A wide mountain valley with snowy peaks, a braided river, and evergreen trees in the foreground, for a piece on showing who stands in the landscape of the work.
caption: A valley you could point to. An about page should be this locatable. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Who belongs on a nonprofit about page?
faqs.answer: People who touch a participant or a donor, and who agree to be public. Program leads, intake, and the person accountable for the report. A grid of untitled retreat photos does not state a duty. Name the decision each role is trusted to make.

faqs.question: How should governance appear?
faqs.answer: In a few plain sentences. How the board is chosen, where this year's report lives, and who reads a concern. Link the report by year and test the file. A dead Financials link is a common crack in an otherwise careful page.

faqs.question: What if staff have changed since the photos?
faqs.answer: Replace the photos or take them down. A warm picture of people who no longer open the door is still false, and a participant will feel it at intake. Review the page when roles change, not only at the next redesign.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A nonprofit about page shows that specific people stand behind the work. A donor or a participant deciding whether the work is real wants to know who does it and why that should matter to them. They are choosing whether to give, join, or read the program. An origin story that does not change that choice can be a sentence, or it can be absent.

Write the page as accountability. Roles, place, and the decisions those people are trusted to make. Warmth is welcome. Vagueness is not. A reader who has seen too many mission statements will look here for a human name attached to a program they might enter.

## Who does the work

Name the roles that touch a participant or a donor. Who answers a new inquiry. Who runs the program on the day it happens. Who watches the money. You do not need every board member on day one. You need the path from "I might show up" to "someone is responsible" to be visible.

Use real names when the organization is small enough that names stay true, and when those people agree to be public. A program lead, an intake coordinator, an executive director who still reads the hard cases. If turnover is high, name the role and the site, and name a person only where a person is the actual promise. A page of faces from two directors ago is a quiet lie.

Say what each role decides. "The clinic lead decides whether a Tuesday list can take another matter." "The finance lead signs the report linked from this page." Decision plus role is the sentence that helps. A hobby, a favorite quote, and a headshot with no duty do not help a person who is about to rely on you.

Board and advisors belong when they change trust. A board that includes the community you serve, a treasurer with a named background, a clinical supervisor. List them in a way that states the duty. A grid of untitled portraits from a retreat does not state a duty. If a person is decorative on the page and absent in governance, leave them off.

## Why a donor or a participant should care

Connect the people to the visitor's risk. A participant's risk is showing up and finding the program thinner than the website. A donor's risk is funding a story that the staff cannot deliver. The about page should reduce those risks with facts. How long this program has run in this place. Who is present during open hours. What supervision or license exists, stated accurately. What the staff will not pretend to be.

Skip the compliments. Passionate. Dedicated. Like a family. These words can be true in the room and still fail on the page, because every organization types them. If a fact sits underneath, use the fact. "Two of the three program leads have run this clinic for five seasons" is checkable. "We are passionate about the community" is not.

Place is a reason when place changes access. On a bus line. In the school building families already enter. In a town with no other version of this service. State the place and the consequence. A pin on a map with a poetic caption about roots does not tell someone whether they can get there on a Thursday.

Partners belong here when they share the work. A host site, a clinical partner, a city contract. Say what they do and what you do. A logo bar without duties implies endorsement you may not have and scale you may not want to claim. One accurate sentence per partner is stronger, and it gives a skeptical reader a way to verify you.

## The origin story, under a hard test

Keep a founding story when deleting it would remove a fact the visitor needs. The test is practical. Does this change the decision to give, join, or read the program? A clinic that exists because a specific legal gap was going unmet, and that still limits itself to that gap, passes. A story about a founder's awakening, with no consequence for this season's hours, fails.

If it passes, tell it short. What was missing, what you built, what is still true. Then return to the visitor. The first screen should not be a memoir. A participant looking for tonight's hours will not forgive a long prelude. Put the hours and the path in reach, and let the history sit after the accountability, or in a compact block beside it.

Myths to retire are the ones that center the organization's feelings. We started with nothing but heart. A single donation changed everything. The community became our family. Some of these events happened. They still ask the reader to feel before they understand. Understanding is the respect. Feeling can follow from a true scene.

If the founder has moved on, do not write the page as if they still open the door. Update the story to the people who open it now. Legacy can be one sentence. The current duty is the page.

## Voice and the top of the page

Read the homepage, a program block, and the about page together. One organization should sound like one voice. Plain nouns, the program's name, the city's name. If the about page suddenly becomes a manifesto, the reader hears a special occasion and wonders what you sound like on an ordinary Tuesday, which is the day they would call.

Give the page a title that says who it is about. The browser title can be the organization plus a plain phrase. The heading on the page can name the people and the program, not "About us," which could belong to anyone. [Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for descriptive, concise titles and a main heading that is obviously the main heading. A row of slogans at the top makes that job harder for a reader and muddier for search.

[Google's people-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) also asks that a visitor be able to tell who created the work and who is responsible. This page is the natural place to answer. Legal name, the place you operate, and a way to reach a person. A nickname and a collage are not an identity. They are an atmosphere.

Write the way intake speaks. If staff say "the pantry" and the page says "nourishment initiative," change the page. The about page is a poor place to introduce a new dialect. People arrive here to confirm they have found the same organization a friend described.

## Photographs with permission

Use pictures of the work and of the people who agreed to represent it. A program lead at the desk they actually use. Volunteers in the task, not lined up in matching shirts against a brick wall, unless that gathering is the true scene. Consent is not a detail. For participants, the default is not to be the illustration. Offer a path that does not depend on their faces.

Staff photos should match the people a visitor might meet. If the page shows a team that has since left, replace the photos or take them down. A warm falsehood is still false, and a participant will feel it at the door. Date the page quietly if turnover is part of your reality, and review it when roles change.

Skip the sad photograph here too. The about page is not the place to prove need by showing someone at their worst. Need can be stated. The work can be shown. A person seeking help is not a prop for the credibility of the helpers. If you lack photos, use fewer images. Strong roles and a clear next step will carry the page.

## Governance, money, and the report

A short, plain account of governance helps a donor who is almost convinced. How the board is chosen, in one sentence. Where the latest report lives. Who signs it. You are not writing a legal treatise. You are showing that the organization can point at its own paperwork without flinching.

If you file a public return or publish an annual report, link it by name and year. "Financials" as a dead label, pointing at a missing file, is a common crack. Test the link. If the report is late, say when it will be posted, and leave last year's file up with the year visible. Absence plus silence is worse than a dated document.

Say how to raise a concern. A participant or a donor who has a problem should see a path that is not the same cheerful form as a volunteer application. An email for the board chair, or a named role, with a sentence about what happens next. Organizations that hide this path look like they have never imagined being wrong. Readers notice.

## Hand the reader a next step

End where the rest of the site ends. Give, join, or read the program. Use the same verbs. A unique "join our family" form with a dozen fields undoes the clarity you just earned. Point to one program that is open and to the report if the reader still wants proof of scale.

Keep the contact facts identical to the contact page. Address, hours, the inbox a person reads. Every inconsistency looks like two organizations. Small teams create these inconsistencies by editing one page on a tired night. Read both pages in one sitting before you publish.

If you want help making the accountable version the public version, start from [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the current about page and the list of who actually runs this season's programs. The work is to put those people on the page in the same voice as the offer, and to leave the myth on the cutting room floor when it does not change a decision.

A reader who trusts the people will ask for a job that shows those people under a real constraint. [Proof pages for a nonprofit](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-nonprofit) are the next piece, because a staff list still has to be backed by the work in the world: what was hard, what you decided, and what a similar donor or participant can do next.
